specAnchors.text: be able to calculate solution concentrations, in mol dm -3 and g dm -3 , including simple acid-base titrations using the indicators methyl orange and phenolphthalein
understand how to minimise the sources of measurement uncertainty in volumetric analysis and estimate the overall uncertainty in the calculated result

primer.text: A titration converts a colour change into a concentration. This note pairs the two standard indicators with their colour switches, runs the four-step calculation from titre volume to unknown molarity, and closes with the uncertainty arithmetic: which readings double their error and how per-equipment percentages stack into one total.

modules.title: Indicators and their colour switches
modules.opening: An indicator is a weak acid-base pair whose two forms wear different colours. This lesson tabulates litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein, and explains why the sharpest switch at the equivalence point decides which indicator a titration can use.
keyPoints: Indicators change colour reversibly as the hydrogen ion concentration shifts.
Each indicator is a weak acid or base whose conjugate forms carry different colours.
Litmus runs red in acid to blue in alkali, methyl orange red to yellow, phenolphthalein colourless to pink.
A good indicator flips sharply exactly at the equivalence point.
Litmus fails in titrations because its change is too gradual to mark an endpoint.

low.restatement: Three common indicators, three colour pairs: memorise the table and you can name the environment from a single drop's colour.
low.analogy: Traffic lights for chemists: each indicator is a light tuned to switch at its own acidity threshold, and only the sharpest lights are useful for spotting the exact crossing point.
low.examPointer: Quote the colour pairs in the right direction - red-acid to blue/yellow-alkali, and colourless-acid to pink-alkali for phenolphthalein.

medium.restatement: The conjugate acid and base forms of an indicator absorb different wavelengths, so the H+ concentration selects which form dominates; a titration indicator must transition within the steep pH jump at equivalence, which is why litmus's wide transition band disqualifies it.
medium.analogy: A swing that tips at one precise weight (equivalence) versus a ramp that drifts across a wide range (litmus) - titrations need the swing.
medium.examPointer: When asked why phenolphthalein goes in the burette, answer about visibility: the sudden appearance of pink is easier to see than pink fading to colourless.

modules.title: From titre to concentration
modules.opening: The titration calculation is a four-step march: balanced equation, moles from titre, stoichiometric scaling, concentration. This lesson runs the sodium carbonate-hydrochloric acid worked example end to end, then converts the answer into grams per dm3.
keyPoints: Concentration is the amount of solute dissolved in one dm3 of solution.
Moles equal concentration times volume in dm3, with cm3 divided by 1000.
The worked example neutralises 25.0 cm3 of 0.050 mol dm-3 sodium carbonate with 20.00 cm3 of acid.
The 1:2 stoichiometry doubles the carbonate's moles to give the HCl moles.
Dividing moles by 0.020 dm3 gives the acid concentration of 0.125 mol dm-3.

low.restatement: Convert the titre to dm3, multiply by concentration to get moles, scale by the equation's ratio, then divide by the unknown's volume to read its concentration.
low.analogy: A recipe scaling: one pan's contents (known solution) is measured, the recipe's ratio (stoichiometry) tells how much the other pan holds, and dividing by its size gives the strength.
low.examPointer: Divide cm3 by 1000 before multiplying - the unit slip is the most common titration-calculation error.

medium.restatement: The stoichiometric coefficient is the multiplier between the known and unknown moles: 0.00125 mol of carbonate at ratio 1:2 yields 0.00250 mol of acid, and 0.00250 / 0.0200 = 0.125 mol dm-3 closes the chain.
medium.analogy: Gear train: the known gear's turns (moles) multiplied by the gear ratio (coefficients) drives the unknown gear; its speed per litre is the concentration.
medium.examPointer: Write the ratio statement '1 mol Na2CO3 reacts with 2 mol HCl' before scaling - the explicit ratio line carries the marks.

modules.title: Stacking the uncertainties
modules.opening: Errors multiply where readings pair up. This lesson distinguishes percentage uncertainty from percentage error, shows why two readings double the absolute uncertainty, and sums the titration apparatus's four contributions into one total.
keyPoints: Percentage uncertainty divides the total uncertainty by the measured value and multiplies by 100.
Percentage error compares a result with a literature value - a different quantity entirely.
Adding or subtracting measurements adds their absolute uncertainties.
A burette reading needs two readings, so its quantity carries twice the single-reading uncertainty.
The titration example sums 0.5, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4 percent into a 1.2 percent total.

low.restatement: Every doubled reading doubles the absolute uncertainty, and the total experiment error is the plain sum of each instrument's percentage contribution.
low.analogy: Four leaky taps each dripping a fixed amount: fill one bucket twice from one tap (double drip) or once from four taps (four drips) - either way the drips add up.
low.examPointer: Keep the two percentages apart: uncertainty compares to your own measurement, error compares to the literature - mixing them loses the mark.

medium.restatement: Each instrument contributes its percentage uncertainty to the propagated total because addition of quantities adds absolute uncertainties; the burette's two readings are already priced into its contribution.
medium.analogy: A relay team's total time is the sum of each runner's time, however fast individuals run - propagation adds contributions, never averages them.
medium.examPointer: Quote the four percentages - balance 0.5, flask 0.1, pipette 0.2, burette 0.4 - and their 1.2 percent total; the explicit addition line carries the method mark.

glossary.definition: The added-reagent amount at which the reactants are in exact stoichiometric proportion, marked by a sharp indicator flip.
The total uncertainty divided by the measured value, times 100.
The burette volume delivered between the initial and final readings, carrying the sum of both readings' uncertainties.

workedExample.prompt: 25.0 cm3 of 0.050 mol dm-3 sodium carbonate is completely neutralised by 20.00 cm3 of dilute hydrochloric acid. Calculate the acid's concentration in mol dm-3.
steps: Step 1 - balanced equation: Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2.
Step 2 - moles of carbonate: multiply 0.025 by 0.050 to get 0.00125 mol.
Step 3 - stoichiometry: the ratio is 1:2, so the acid moles are 2 x 0.00125 = 0.00250 mol.
Step 4 - concentration: 0.00250 mol / 0.0200 dm3 = 0.125 mol dm-3.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The hydrochloric acid concentration is 0.125 mol dm-3.
